newsitem.title: UK: Copper traders see Asian openings post-Hamanaka.
newsitem.headline: Copper traders see Asian openings post-Hamanaka.

text.p: Physical copper traders based in London have seen enquiries from Asian customers increase since the dismissal of Sumitomo Corp's former star trader Yasuo Hamanaka in June.

But business remains extremely competitive, with major merchants and low-cost copper producers best placed to fill gaps left by any Sumitomo retrenchment in the Asian physical copper markets, traders, merchants and producers said.
"Yes, opportunities have opened up in Asia for us," said a senior trader with a major Western merchant. "But now it's a question of turning those opportunities into real business."
"It is not affecting the spot market so much now, but medium term we will have more enquiries in Asia," a producer added.

On Tuesday Sumitomo announced plunging copper sales during the first half of the 1996/97 business year, sending a signal to copper traders that the conglomerate may be cutting back its role in the Asian physical copper market.
Sumitomo said it does not plan to withdraw altogether, although it may not be as competitive on pricing as previously.
The announcement came as no surprise to Western traders who believed Hamanaka sold cut-price copper on the physical markets while seeking to cover this by profiting in copper derivatives.
This helped explain the dominance of one individual over world copper markets for the best part of a decade, they said.

"We saw Sumitomo trading at what we considered to be irrational terms," the merchant said. "There is now a lot of uncertainty among Asian copper consumers now that Sumitomo have withdrawn their charitable dealings."
Traders said maintaining a tight grip on the markets in this way was always going to run into trouble eventually.

"Sumitomo did undercut the market to a certain extent, but you can only take advantage of this near term if you have a game plan," said one physical trader at an LME ring dealing firm. "You can't sustain it in the long term, as Hamanaka has proved."

In June Sumitomo announced $1.8 billion losses in unauthorised copper trading which it has since alleged was masterminded by Hamanaka, once dubbed "Mr Five Percent" for the percentage of the copper markets he controlled.
The loss has since been revised to $2.6 billion.
The main beneficiaries of Hamanaka's downfall are expected to be low-cost producers like Chile's state-owned Codelco.
"We have seen the knock-on effect to a small extent," said another London-based trader.
"But you have to remember that there is new production coming on stream and being offered cheaply - especially SX-EW (solvent-extraction, electrowinning) material," he added.
"This will go a long way to filling the gap."

SX-EW is a fast-expanding and very cheap method of producing copper. According to estimates from Billiton Metals, SX-EW output increased from around 250,000 tonnes in 1985 to 1.25 million ten years later.
"This figure will virtually double by the end of the century," Billiton said in a recent report.
Major merchants who can deal in large tonnages may also benefit from a freer Asian marketplace, traders said.
London traders expected Sumitomo to continue to operate in the Asian physical markets through long-term contracts, but added it was unlikely to enjoy the dominance it once had.
"They'll have long-term contracts against supply contracts," said one. "But they are not the force they used to be."
